text: Resolution No. 4 (New Series). COMMUNICATION FROM CITY AND COUNTY OFFICERS. Headquarters Certain Officials. The following Communication was received and read-: San Francisco, April 23, 1906. The City Attorney, Auditor, Treasurer, Tax Collector and County Recorder held a meeting this day at the hour of ten o'clock at 2513 Sacramento street, near Fillmore, and formally organized themselves into a Commission for the purpose of selecting and fitting up offices for their respective duties. On motion of Tax Collector Nichols, City Attorney Burke was duly elected Chairman of the Commission, and on motion of Treasurer Bantel, Samuel Wells Horton, Auditor, was duly elected as Secretary, Maurice L. Asher, Attorney for the Auditor, representing him in his absence. On motion of Tax Collector Nichols, it was resolved that the buildings known as 2511 and 2513 Sacramento street, near Fillmore street, consisting of twenty spacious rooms, be engaged and selected at once as the offices of the aforesaid respective officials. It was further resolved that the offices be fitted up at once, that the Mayor of the City and County of San Francisco be notified of the action of the Commission with a request for his approval of their action. On motion of Treasurer Bantel, it was resolved that business of the respective officials of the Commission begin at once, and all employees be requested to report for duty Tuesday, April 24, 1906. The Commission then adjourned to meet at their newly selected headquarters Tuesday, April 24th, at 10 o'clock a. m. WILLIAM G. BURKE, Chairman. S. W. HORTON, Secretary.

text: Motion. Supervisor Boxton moved that those interested in the matter before the Board be granted the privilege of the floor. So ordered. Privilege of the Floor. Garret McEnerney, Attorney, representing P. W. Riordan, Roman Catholic Archbishop of San Francisco and the South of Market Street Propertyowners' Association, addressed the Board, opposing the extension of the Fire Limits, as proposed by the Committee. The gentleman stated that the idea of the fire limits was that if a wooden building was burned it should be replaced by a fireproof building, but that as conditions are now entirely changed by reason of the calamity, such a proposition would be an onerous one to the small propertyowner. It would mean that the householder cannot go back to the place which was once his home. He believed the present limits were too extensive in area, but this condition cannot be changed except by charter amendment, inasmuch as the law provides that the fire limits cannot be changed except by extension. If the limits were extended it would be equivalent to confiscation of property Oi. small holders, and in conclusion the gentleman asked that no change be made from the existing limits. George D. Shadburne, Attorney, representing property-owners west of Stockton street and north of Bush street, was heard objecting to the extension of the Fire Limits in that direction. John R. Bride, representing Larkin and Polk street property-owners, opposed the extension of the Fire Limits to include said streets. Rev. Father Mulligan, pastor of St. Joseph's Church, and Rev. Father Rogers, pastor of St. Patrick's Church, addressed the Board, objecting to the extension of the fire limits south of Market street, on the ground that it would be practically confiscation of the property of poor people. SITE FOR STATE BUILDING IN SAN FRANCISCO. Statement. The Chair stated that the Legislature of the State of California had under consideration a proposition to appropriate moneys for the construction of a State Building in San Francisco, and that in connection therewith it had been suggested by members of the Legislature that the City and County either donate or lease sufficient land to the State for the erection thereon of said Building. Inasmuch as the Legislature is now in session, action must be taken at once if the Board favored the proposition. LIQUOR LICENSE. Message from Mayor, Relative to Imposition of Liquor License and to Regulations Concerning Sale of Liquors. To the Honorable Board of Supervisors— Gentlemen: The solution of a grave and serious problem confronts you, and on account of its importance to you, to the interests affected and to the people of the city at large, I venture a few recommendations by way of suggestion as to the line, of policy proper to be pursued. With the beginning of the new fiscal year on July first, it is advisable to begin the administ;^ation with what will soon be our new and greater San Francisco with a clean page as to the many matters of consequence, but perhaps none will be of as much significance and of so far reaching result as our official treatment of the liquor traffic. Before proceeding, however, I wish to state that we must approach the decision of this question in a sane and rational manner. We must not allow ourselves to be misled in judgment by the prejudiced appeals of the extremist, nor yet to be entirely carried away by the claims of sympathy. In the face of the catastrophe which has come to us all with equal loss and with equal force, let us be just and fair to the individual affected, and at the same time have due regard to uhe best interests of the city which we shall now earnestly strive to restore and to rebuild, even beyond her former greatness, and in this great work we must rely on the earnest and sincere cooperation, under trying conditions, both of the liquor dealers of San Francisco and of those who have stood against them. On the eighteenth of April, 1906, I issued a Proclamation closing the saloons and stopping the sale of liquor in Safi Francisco. The order then issued is yet in force. The result has had so marked and beneficial an effect as justly to be termed almost marvelous. It was an emergency measure, framed to meet a time of abnormal excitement under which men might easily have been carried away from their ordinary habits, and without consideration of results, have been led into excesses. Ana I am pleased to say that no body of men concurred in the position I then assumed relative to this traffic, or more commended it, than the liquor dealers themselves; nor did any of our fellow citizens as a body more earnestly support me in maintaining me desired conditions aimed at, than did the very men whose property, income and livlihood were most injuriously affected thereby. text: Motion. Supervisor Boxton moved that all parties interested be granted the privilege of the floor. So ordered. Privilege of Floor. F B. Carson, attorney, representing Protestants against reduction of grade, was heard at length in opposition to the pending measure, and presented, read and filed the following protests: , ,. 1 Of Red Men's Hall Association and" other property owners against lowering the grade of Golden Gate avenue. 2. Of Wm. A. Schultz and other property owners against changing grade of Golden Gate avenue, unless Leavenworth street is extended to Market street. 3. Of L. E. Clawson and other propert' owners, against lowering grade of Golden Gate avenue, unless Leavenworth street is extended to Market street. J. H. Hutaflf, representing Red Men's Hall Association, was heard in opposition to the change of grade, stating that it was the intention of the Association to rebuild its properties on Golden Gate avenue at great expense, and that they desired no obstacle to be placed in the way. Adolph Meyer, property owner opposed the present plan of changing the grade on the ground that it was not properly distributed in front of the properties affected. Father Valentine, representing St. Boniface Church, opposed changing the grade on the ground thCcC it would cause great loss and inconvenience to his church. Chas. W. Lynch, attorney representing protestants, was heard at length relative to the procedure involved in the matter of changing the grade of Golden Gate avenue, and held that inasmuch as the avenue was an accepted street, the expense of doing the work devolved upon the City and County. F. B. Carson, resuming his argument, stated that Attorney Jas. A. Devoto of the Board of Public Works advised that if the grade was changed the expense must be borne by the City, and in conclusion asked that the petition to change the grade be denied on this ground. Joseph S. Tobin, representing proponents of the plan of reducing the grade, was heard at length favoring the proposition. Thos. B. Woodward, City Engineer, explained the method of establishing the proposed grade, and stated that the total estimated cost would be $130,000, of which $90,000 would be expended in street work and $40,000 in grading of lots. Jas. D. Phelan, proponent of measure, addressed the Board, favoring changing grade on the ground of great public benefit.
plain_line: Property owners protest lowering the Golden Gate Avenue grade
